summary: A 1978 extension to the SUPDUP protocol that adds graphics support, so a remote host can draw pictures on a user's display. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 746 proposes a graphics extension to SUPDUP, so remote programs can draw on a terminal as well as send text. It uses the existing SUPDUP output connection and lets terminals report which graphics features they support.

subtitle: A proposal for sending graphics commands through the ordinary SUPDUP output connection.

tldr.problem: SUPDUP handles text, but programs also need a terminal-independent way to display drawings on programmable terminals.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds a graphics mode with commands for lines, points, rectangles and characters, using the normal text output connection and terminal capability bits.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says the extension had not been implemented and publishes it to request suggestions and encourage an implementation.

today: The unit records RFC 746's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The RFC says the SUPDUP graphics extension had not been implemented when the proposal was published.

sections.title: Adding Graphics to SUPDUP
sections.content:
The proposal extends SUPDUP to display drawings as well as text. A program on the server can begin sending graphics without special preparation, and graphics commands travel through the normal text output connection, so no additional network connection is needed.

The author says the extension is intended to work with locally connected intelligent terminals as well as remote terminals. It defines a standard graphics command language so server programs do not need terminal-specific conversion software.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension lets a server send drawing instructions over the same connection it uses for text. Programs can use a shared command language instead of writing special code for each terminal.

sections.title: Entering Graphics Mode and Drawing
sections.content:
A terminal reports graphics support through the optional SMARTS variable. The server enters graphics mode with %TDGRF; characters from 0 through 177 octal are then interpreted as graphics commands. A character at least 200 octal exits graphics mode and returns to its usual interpretation.

The command set includes drawing and erasing lines, points, rectangles and character strings, plus commands to move the graphics cursor, clear the screen, select object sets and request cursor input. A graphics cursor is separate from the normal text cursor and uses dot coordinates. Each coordinate is a 14-bit signed number; terminals may also support virtual coordinates scaled to the display.
sections.plainLanguage: A special code starts graphics mode, where the terminal reads drawing commands from the output stream. The graphics cursor uses screen dots, and a separate code returns the stream to normal interpretation.

sections.title: Terminal Capabilities and Object Sets
sections.content:
The SMARTS variable reports optional capabilities such as graphics, multiple object sets, rectangles, XOR drawing, blinking and virtual coordinates. Some terminals can also return a cursor position or redirect output to a hard-copy device.

A terminal may support sets of graphics objects that can be shown, hidden or moved together. Programs can save and restore input-stream state so several processes can draw on one terminal without overwriting each other's cursor and mode settings. The author notes that some features, including sets, may not be practical on bit-matrix terminals.
sections.plainLanguage: Terminals can report which features they have, so a program can use only supported operations. Object sets and saved state can help several programs share one display.

sections.title: Implementation Status and Limits
sections.content:
The author states that the extension had never been implemented and says it is published to solicit suggestions and encourage someone to try it. The terminal does not need to remember the semantic structure of a picture; it may draw lines and points or represent the image as a bit matrix.

The proposal deliberately leaves some device features unspecified and says additional features should wait until they are needed and understood. Graphics commands may be stored in text files, but the RFC notes that doing so does not preserve the relationships or internal data a picture-editing program may need.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes a proposed protocol and says it had not yet been implemented. It focuses on displaying graphics, not preserving all the editing information a drawing program may use.
